definitions.definition: The extinguishing of greed, hatred and delusion (SN 38.1), the unconditioned (SN 43.12; AN 3.47), the cessation of becoming (SN 12.68), described by negation as the sphere without elements, formless spheres, worlds, coming or going (Ud 8.1) and as the unborn, unmade (Ud 8.3); realised in this life (with residue) and at death (without residue) (Iti 44); not a self (MN 1; Dhp 279).
The one unconditioned ultimate reality (paramattha-dhamma), with the characteristic of peace; distinct from mere absence (commentarial).

relations.note: liberation as each tradition defines it; Theravāda denies that nibbāna is the self or Brahman
the arahant's living nibbāna versus the final passing

definitions.definition: The unconditioned is taught under thirty-three names — the uninclined, taintless, truth, far shore, subtle, very hard to see, unaging, stable, undisintegrating, unmanifest, unproliferated, peaceful, deathless, sublime, auspicious, secure, destruction of craving, wonderful, amazing, unailing, nibbāna, unafflicted, dispassion, purity, freedom, unadhesive, island, shelter, asylum, refuge, destination (SN 43.12–44).
With residue remaining (the living arahant who still experiences the agreeable and disagreeable) and without residue remaining (when all that is felt becomes cool at death) (Iti 44).

The final passing of the Buddha or an arahant; the Buddha passed up through the jhānas and formless attainments to cessation, down again, and attained final nibbāna on emerging from the fourth jhāna (DN 16); what happens to the Tathāgata after it is undeclared (MN 72).

Whether the Tathāgata exists, does not exist, both or neither after death is undeclared: liberated from reckoning by form and the other aggregates he is deep like the ocean, and 'reborn' or 'not reborn' does not apply (MN 72); since he is not apprehended in truth even here, annihilation cannot be asserted (SN 22.85–86).

The end of the world cannot be reached by travelling, yet there is no end of suffering without reaching it; the world, its origin, cessation and way are declared in this fathom-long body with its perception and mind (SN 2.26).
At the death of the arahant Vakkali (and Godhika) Māra searches for his consciousness in vain; he attained final nibbāna with consciousness unestablished (SN 22.87).

'This mind is luminous, defiled by adventitious defilements'; the ordinary person does not understand this, so there is no development of mind for him; the noble disciple does (AN 1.51–52). The commentary identifies the luminous mind with the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) (U37).

relations.note: later Mahāyāna texts cite a luminous mind; the Pali passage does not posit an innate buddha-nature
the commentarial identification with the life-continuum (U37)

definitions.definition: Suffering, its origin (craving), its cessation, and the path (the noble eightfold path) (SN 56.11); to be fully understood, abandoned, realised and developed; what the Buddha declares because it is beneficial (MN 63; SN 56.31); all wholesome states are included in them as footprints in an elephant's (MN 28).

Each truth known as 'this is …', 'it is to be (understood / abandoned / realised / developed)', and 'it has been …' — three turnings × four truths = twelve aspects; only when this knowledge was purified did the Buddha claim awakening (SN 56.11).

The practice that avoids devotion to sensual pleasure and self-mortification — the noble eightfold path (SN 56.11); the balanced energy of the lute (AN 6.55); in doctrine the middle between 'all exists' and 'all does not exist', i.e. dependent origination (SN 12.15).

relations.note: the self-mortification rejected in SN 56.11 and MN 36

definitions.definition: Right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration (SN 45.8); contained in the three trainings (MN 44); right view comes first and each factor has a mundane and a supramundane form (MN 117); where it is found, the four kinds of ascetic are found (DN 16).

Training in higher virtue, higher mind and higher wisdom (AN 3.89); speech, action and livelihood belong to virtue, effort, mindfulness and concentration to concentration, view and intention to wisdom (MN 44); virtue and wisdom purify each other (DN 4).

relations.note: U51's map

definitions.definition: The step-by-step path of the suttas: faith and going forth, virtue, sense restraint, mindfulness and clear comprehension, contentment, seclusion, abandoning the hindrances, the four jhānas, the direct knowledges and the destruction of the effluents (DN 2; MN 27; MN 39; MN 107); final knowledge comes by gradual training, not at once (MN 70); the ocean slopes gradually (Ud 5.5).

name: The thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (bodhipakkhiyā dhammā)

definitions.definition: Seven groups taught for the long endurance of the holy life: the four establishments of mindfulness, four right efforts, four bases of power, five faculties, five powers, seven factors of awakening and the noble eightfold path (DN 16; MN 149; SN 43).

relations.note: the same thirty-seven in the Sarvāstivāda sources (U38)

notes: Each of the 37 has its own term entry (trm:kayanupassana … trm:samma-samadhi).

definitions.definition: Contemplating body, feelings, mind and dhammas, ardent, clearly comprehending and mindful, having removed covetousness and grief for the world (MN 10); fulfilled by mindfulness of breathing and fulfilling the awakening factors (MN 118); one's own pasture (SN 47.6).
Restraining unarisen unwholesome states, abandoning arisen ones, developing unarisen wholesome states and maintaining arisen ones; identical with right effort (SN 45.8).
Concentration through desire, energy, mind and investigation, with formations of striving, developed without slackness or tension (SN 51.20); for a monk, 'long life' (DN 26).
A basis for the powers and for the destruction of the effluents (SN 51.20; DN 26).

name: The five faculties and five powers

definitions.definition: Faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration and wisdom (SN 48.10); as powers they cannot be shaken by their opposites.

relations.note: YS 1.20 lists śraddhā, vīrya, smṛti, samādhi, prajñā

definitions.definition: Energy must be neither too tight nor too slack, like lute strings; one should penetrate the evenness of the faculties (AN 6.55; Vin Mv 5.1); the bases of power are developed without slackness or tension (SN 51.20).

Mindfulness, investigation of dhammas, energy, rapture, tranquillity, concentration, equanimity; arising in sequence from the establishments of mindfulness and fulfilling true knowledge and liberation (MN 118); nourished and starved by attention (SN 46.51); to be applied according to whether the mind is sluggish or restless (SN 46.53).

Calm and insight developed together — insight preceded by calm, calm by insight, or yoked evenly (AN 4.170; MN 149); calm and insight are the path to the unconditioned (SN 43.12); no jhāna without wisdom, no wisdom without jhāna (Dhp 372); the jhānas as a basis for insight into the aggregates (MN 64; AN 9.36).

For a pleasant abiding here and now (the jhānas), for knowledge and vision (perception of light), for mindfulness and clear comprehension (knowing feelings, perceptions and thoughts arise and pass), and for the destruction of the effluents (rise and fall of the aggregates) (AN 4.41).

name: Transcendental dependent origination (upanisā)

definitions.definition: Suffering is the proximate cause of faith, faith of gladness, gladness of rapture, rapture of tranquillity, tranquillity of happiness, happiness of concentration, concentration of knowledge and vision of things as they are, that of disenchantment, that of dispassion, that of liberation, liberation of the knowledge of destruction (SN 12.23); a parallel sequence from virtue (AN 11.1–2).

notes: The name 'transcendental dependent origination' is modern-commentarial usage; the text calls the links upanisā.

definitions.definition: Purification of virtue, of mind, of view, by overcoming doubt, by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path, by knowledge and vision of the way, and knowledge and vision — each serving the next like a relay of chariots, the goal being final nibbāna without clinging (MN 24); systematised in the Visuddhimagga (U37).

relations.note: systematised by the Visuddhimagga (U37)

name: The four stages of awakening and the eight noble persons

definitions.definition: Stream-enterer (three fetters abandoned), once-returner (lust, hatred, delusion attenuated), non-returner (five lower fetters abandoned) and arahant (all ten), each with a path and a fruit — eight noble persons, four pairs (DN 16; MN 64; Ud 5.5); women and men alike can realise all four fruits (Cv 10.1.3).

relations.note: the Abhidhamma presentation of path and fruit (U37)

definitions.definition: Those on the path to and in the fruit of stream-entry, once-return, non-return and arahantship — the Saṅgha of the four pairs (AN 6.10; Snp 2.1; Ud 5.5).
Freed both ways, freed by wisdom, body-witness, attained to view, freed by faith, Dhamma-follower, faith-follower — distinguished by formless attainment, wisdom and faith (MN 70).

For stream-entry: association with good persons, hearing the true Dhamma, wise attention, practice in accordance (SN 55.5); of the stream-enterer: confirmed confidence in the Buddha, Dhamma and Saṅgha and the virtues dear to the noble ones — the mirror of the Dhamma (DN 16).

name: The ten factors of the arahant

definitions.definition: The eight path factors with right knowledge and right liberation (MN 117).

name: Seven stations of consciousness and two spheres

definitions.definition: Kinds of beings by body and perception (diverse in body and perception such as humans, … the spheres of infinite space, consciousness and nothingness) and the two spheres of non-percipient beings and neither-perception-nor-non-perception; understanding them one is freed by wisdom (DN 15).

Seeing forms while having form, seeing forms externally, being intent on 'beautiful', the four formless spheres and the cessation of perception and feeling; one who enters and emerges from them and has destroyed the effluents is 'freed both ways' (DN 15; DN 16).

First jhāna: secluded from sensual pleasures and unwholesome states, with applied and sustained thought, rapture and bliss born of seclusion; second: with inner confidence and unification, rapture and bliss born of concentration; third: equanimous, mindful, clearly comprehending, feeling bliss; fourth: neither pleasant nor painful, purity of mindfulness through equanimity (DN 2; SN 45.8) — each with its simile of bodily pervasion; right concentration.

relations.note: the Yoga Sūtra's samādhi with vitarka and vicāra shares vocabulary; the two traditions do not identify their states

definitions.definition: Secluded from sensual pleasures and unwholesome states, with applied and sustained thought, rapture and bliss born of seclusion, pervading the body like bath powder kneaded with water (DN 2); remembered by the bodhisatta from childhood (MN 36); lust is abandoned through it (MN 44).
With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, inner confidence and unification of mind, rapture and bliss born of concentration, like a lake fed from within by a spring (DN 2).
With the fading of rapture, equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, feeling bliss with the body — 'equanimous and mindful, one dwells in bliss' — like lotuses immersed in cool water (DN 2).

With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, neither painful nor pleasant, with purity of mindfulness through equanimity, the body pervaded by the pure bright mind like a man wrapped in white cloth (DN 2); the basis for the direct knowledges and the point from which the Buddha attained final nibbāna (DN 16).

The spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness and neither-perception-nor-non-perception, reached by passing beyond perceptions of form (MN 111; MN 121); the bodhisatta learned the third and fourth from Āḷāra and Uddaka and rejected them as not leading to nibbāna (MN 26); each is a basis for insight (AN 9.36).

The cessation of perception and feeling, beyond the formless spheres: verbal, bodily and mental formations cease in that order, while vitality and heat remain, unlike a dead person (MN 43; MN 44); reached through the progressive cessation of perception (DN 9); emerged from with the contacts of empty, signless and undirected (MN 44).

name: Death and the attainment of cessation distinguished

definitions.definition: At death bodily, verbal and mental formations cease, vitality is exhausted, heat dissipated and the faculties broken up; in cessation the formations cease but vitality and heat remain and the faculties are clear (MN 43).

name: The kinds of liberation of mind

definitions.definition: Immeasurable, through nothingness, emptiness and signless liberations of mind, which differ in name but are one in meaning in that the unshakeable liberation is empty of lust, hatred and delusion, the 'makers of measure, something and signs' (MN 43).

The world is empty of self and of what belongs to self (SN 35.85); a meditative dwelling in which what is absent is seen as empty and what remains as present, descending to the signless and liberation (MN 121); dwelling in emptiness internally (MN 122); 'look upon the world as empty' (Snp 5.16).

relations.note: Madhyamaka universalises emptiness as lack of own-nature of all dharmas; the suttas speak of emptiness of self

definitions.definition: Perception of light and vision of forms arising in concentration and vanishing when the imperfections of concentration arise; the bodhisatta abandoned eleven imperfections to stabilise them (MN 128); the perception of light is a development of concentration leading to knowledge and vision (AN 4.41).
Psychic powers, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, the divine eye and the destruction of the effluents, attainable from the fourth jhāna (DN 2; AN 3.101; MN 119).

relations.note: the powers may be attained, but their display is disparaged (DN 11)

definitions.definition: Recollection of past lives, the divine eye and the destruction of the effluents, attained by the Buddha in the three watches of the night of awakening (MN 4; MN 36); the Buddhist 'three Vedas' (DN 13).

The wonders of psychic power, of revealing others' minds, and of instruction; the Buddha is horrified by the first two, which an unbeliever may ascribe to a charm, and praises only the wonder of instruction (DN 11); a monk is rebuked for displaying power to laypeople (Vin Cv 5.8).

name: The ten powers of a Tathāgata

definitions.definition: Knowledge of the possible and impossible, of the results of kamma, of the ways leading everywhere, of the world of many elements, of beings' inclinations, of their faculties, of the defilement and purification of meditative attainments, of past lives, of beings' passing and rebirth, and of the destruction of the effluents (MN 12).

One awakened by himself to the Dhamma, not a god, gandhabba, yakkha or human, having abandoned the effluents (AN 4.36); endowed with ten powers and four confidences (MN 12); the rediscoverer of an ancient path (SN 12.65); one of a line of Buddhas (DN 14).

relations.note: the Buddha of the suttas is not an incarnation of a god; the Purāṇic avatāra reading is an external interpretation

definitions.definition: Seven Buddhas within ninety-one aeons — Vipassī, Sikhī, Vessabhū, Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, Kassapa, Gotama (DN 14); twenty-four from Dīpaṅkara in the Buddhavaṃsa.
The Buddha who will arise when human life has risen again to eighty thousand years (DN 26).

What is natural for a bodhisatta: descent from Tusita, conception and birth with earthquakes and light, a virtuous mother who dies seven days after birth, birth standing, the lion's roar 'this is my last birth', the thirty-two marks (DN 14).

An aspiration made before a living Buddha under eight conditions (Bv 2.59), a prediction, and the fulfilment of the ten perfections over countless aeons (Bv 2; Cp; Jā); in the Nikāyas 'bodhisatta' designates Gotama before his awakening (MN 4, 19, 26, 36).

relations.note: the Mahāyāna makes the bodhisattva path a universal ideal; Theravāda reserves it for aspirants to Buddhahood

definitions.definition: Giving, virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness and equanimity, discerned by Sumedha as the qualities that make a Buddha (Bv 2.116–165); illustrated (seven of them) in the Cariyāpiṭaka.

relations.note: the Mahāyāna six (and ten) pāramitās overlap but differ in members

definitions.definition: An old man, a sick man, a dead man and a renunciant, whose sight moves the bodhisatta (Vipassī in DN 14) to go forth.

Under the Bodhi tree at Uruvelā the Buddha attended to dependent origination in the three watches of the night and uttered the verses on phenomena becoming manifest to the ardent brahmin (Ud 1.1–3; Vin Mv 1.1); the house-builder verses (Dhp 153–154).

After the awakening the Buddha inclined not to teach, the Dhamma being deep and against the stream; Brahmā Sahampati implored him, and seeing beings like lotuses at different depths he opened the doors to the deathless (SN 6.1; MN 26; DN 14; Vin Mv 1.5).

name: The first teaching and the first disciples

definitions.definition: At Isipatana the Buddha taught the five monks the middle way and the four truths (SN 56.11) and not-self (SN 22.59); Koṇḍañña gained the eye of Dhamma, and all five became arahants (Vin Mv 1.6).
Dependent origination and the eightfold path as an ancient path travelled by the Buddhas of old, rediscovered like an overgrown road to a ruined city (SN 12.65).
Whether or not Tathāgatas arise, the element stands — specific conditionality (SN 12.20), the three marks (AN 3.136) — which a Tathāgata discovers and makes known.

The five aggregates are not-self since they lead to affliction and cannot be commanded (SN 22.59), impermanent and so not fit to be regarded as self (SN 22.59; MN 148); neither self nor what belongs to self is found (MN 22); 'a being' is a convention for the aggregates (SN 5.10; Mil 3.1.1); the Buddha declined 'there is a self' and 'there is no self' before Vacchagotta (SN 44.10).

relations.note: the Upaniṣadic and Nyāya self is what the suttas examine and do not find
the Pudgalavāda 'person' neither identical with nor different from the aggregates (U38)

definitions.definition: The Tathāgata uses the world's expressions without grasping them (DN 9); 'being' is a convention like 'chariot' (SN 5.10); in the ultimate sense no person is found (Mil 3.1.1) — the root of the commentarial two truths (sammuti- and paramattha-sacca).

relations.note: the commentarial two truths (sammuti- and paramattha-sacca) build on these passages

definitions.definition: Form, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness, whatever of each is past, future or present (SN 22.48); as aggregates of clinging they are suffering in brief (SN 56.11) and identity (MN 44); like foam, a bubble, a mirage, a plantain trunk and a magic trick (SN 22.95); the burden (SN 22.22).

relations.note: both analyse the person into five, but the aggregates are not layers of a self

definitions.definition: The six internal bases (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind) and six external (forms, sounds, odours, tastes, tangibles, mental objects) — 'the all' (SN 35.23); with the six consciousnesses the eighteen elements (MN 115).
The six sense faculties, six objects and six consciousnesses (MN 115; MN 148).
Earth, water, fire, air, space and consciousness, of which a person consists (MN 140; AN 3.61).
Earth (solidity), water (cohesion), fire (heat), air (motion), internal and external, seen as 'not mine' (MN 28; MN 62); the four vipers (SN 35.238).

relations.note: the Brahmanical and Sāṃkhya lists add space (ākāśa) as a fifth element; the suttas' six-element list adds space and consciousness

name: The thirty-two parts of the body

definitions.definition: Head hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin … urine — reviewed from the soles up and the crown down as a bag of mixed grains (MN 10; MN 119; Khp 3); the brain appears in the Khp list.

The ordinary person conceives each thing — earth to nibbāna — as self, in self, from self or 'mine' and delights in it; the trainee should not conceive; the Tathāgata does not, having understood that delight is the root of suffering (MN 1); 'I am' is a conceiving (MN 140).

Dependent on eye and form eye-consciousness arises; contact, feeling, perception, thinking, and proliferation follow, whence perceptions and notions tinged with proliferation beset a person (MN 18); rooted in 'I am' (Snp 4.14); disputes arise from it (Snp 4.11).
Edible food, contact, mental volition and consciousness, which sustain beings, each with its simile (SN 12.63; MN 9; MN 38).

'When this exists, that comes to be' (SN 12.21): suffering arises through conditions and ceases with their cessation; deep and hard to see (DN 15); whoever sees it sees the Dhamma (MN 28); the middle between existence and non-existence (SN 12.15); it stands whether Tathāgatas arise or not (SN 12.20).

relations.note: Sāṃkhya's pre-existent effect; see dsp:causation
creation by God is one of the three sectarian tenets rejected in AN 3.61

definitions.definition: Ignorance, formations, consciousness, name-and-form, six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, ageing-and-death (SN 12.1–2); DN 15 gives a version in which consciousness and name-and-form condition each other.
All formations are impermanent, all formations are suffering, all phenomena are not-self (AN 3.136; Dhp 277–279); the conditioned shows arising, passing and alteration (AN 3.47).
Clinging to sensual pleasures, views, rules and observances, and a doctrine of self (SN 12.2; MN 11).

Sensual desire, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, doubt — abandoned before the first jhāna (DN 2; MN 39), fed and starved by attention (SN 46.51), like muddied water (SN 46.55).

Identity view, doubt, clinging to rules and vows, sensual lust, ill will (the five lower), lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness, ignorance (the five higher); abandoned stage by stage (MN 64; MN 2).

The theories about the past (eternalism, partial eternalism, finitude, eel-wriggling, chance origin) and the future (percipient, non-percipient, neither, annihilation, nibbāna here and now) listed in the Brahmajāla; all arise from contact and craving (DN 1).

Whether the world is eternal or not, finite or infinite, whether the soul is the same as the body or different, whether the Tathāgata exists after death, does not, both or neither — set aside as not beneficial and not leading to nibbāna (MN 63; MN 72; SN 44.10; DN 9); the blind men and the elephant (Ud 6.4).

The sage of the Aṭṭhakavagga holds no formulated view, does not dispute, does not proclaim 'here alone is purity' and does not take himself as equal, superior or inferior (Snp 4.3, 4.8, 4.9); even right view is a raft (MN 22; MN 38).
The Dhamma is like a raft, for crossing over, not for carrying on one's head; even good states are to be let go of (MN 22); even the pure view of dependent origination is not to be clung to (MN 38).
Learning the Dhamma for criticism and debate is like seizing a snake by the tail (MN 22).

The Evil One, lord of death and sensual desire, who tempts and threatens the Buddha and the nuns (Snp 3.2; SN 4; SN 5), has ten armies (Snp 3.2), and finds no opening in one who roams in his own pasture (SN 47.6) or develops mindfulness of the body (MN 119).
That all experience is due to past deeds, to God's creation, or to no cause — each leading to inaction (AN 3.61).
The domain of the Buddhas, the domain of jhāna, the results of kamma, and speculation about the world (AN 4.77).

What cannot happen: one accomplished in view taking any formation as permanent or self, killing parents or an arahant; two Buddhas in one world; a woman being a fully awakened Buddha, wheel-turning monarch, Sakka, Māra or Brahmā; bad conduct ripening as pleasant (MN 115; AN 1.268–295).
The threefold examination of sensual pleasures, forms and feelings (MN 13).

The monk's virtue of abstentions (DN 1; DN 2), the lay precepts, and the Pātimokkha; its purpose is non-remorse leading on to liberation (AN 11.1); ordinary people praise the Buddha only for it (DN 1).
Abstaining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech and intoxicants — 'five great gifts' of safety to countless beings (AN 8.39).

relations.note: four of the five overlap with the yamas of YS 2.30 and the Jain vows

definitions.definition: On the uposatha the lay follower abstains, like the arahants, from killing, stealing, all sexual activity, lying, intoxicants, eating after midday, entertainment and adornment, and high luxurious beds (AN 8.41).

name: The ten precepts of the novice

definitions.definition: The eight with entertainments and adornment separated and the refusal of gold and silver (Khp 2).
Three bodily (killing, stealing, sexual misconduct), four verbal (lying, divisive, harsh, idle speech) and three mental (covetousness, ill will, wrong view), and their opposites (MN 41; AN 10.176).

The householder's discipline: the six directions and mutual duties, the four defilements of action and four biases, the six drains on wealth, true friends (DN 31); four sources of welfare now and hereafter (AN 8.54); five wrong trades (AN 5.177); the blessings (Snp 2.4).
The thirty-eight (traditional count) highest blessings from not associating with fools to a mind unshaken by worldly conditions (Snp 2.4).
The whole of the holy life (SN 45.2); the first support for the maturing of the mind's liberation (Ud 4.1); true and false friends (DN 31).
Hatred is appeased by non-hatred — an eternal law (Dhp 5; Vin Mv 10.2); love even under the saw (MN 21).
Since each holds himself dearest, one who loves himself should not harm another (Ud 5.1); protecting others protects oneself (SN 47.19).
Protecting oneself one protects others through mindfulness; protecting others one protects oneself through patience, harmlessness, love and sympathy (SN 47.19).

Love, compassion, rejoicing and equanimity pervading all directions without measure (DN 13; MN 62); a divine abiding here (Snp 1.8); the path to the Brahmā world (DN 13) and a basis for liberation of mind (MN 43).

relations.note: YS 1.33's maitrī, karuṇā, muditā, upekṣā; see brw:buddhism-yoga-four-attitudes

definitions.definition: Eleven benefits of the liberation of mind by love — sleeping and waking well, no bad dreams, dear to humans and non-humans, protected by deities, unharmed by fire, poison and weapons, quick concentration, serene complexion, unconfused death, rebirth in the Brahmā world (AN 11.15); it outshines all merit (Iti 27).
Going for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Saṅgha (Khp 1); first the form of ordination (Vin Mv 1.12); the 'jewels' of the Ratana Sutta.
Recollection of the Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha, one's virtue, one's generosity and the deities, by which the mind is not obsessed and becomes concentrated (AN 6.10).
The comforts of one whose mind is free of enmity whether or not there is another world and fruit of deeds (AN 3.65).

Not accepting teachings on tradition, lineage, report, scripture, logic, inference, reasoned reflection, a view, a speaker's competence or respect for a teacher, but on knowing for oneself which states are unwholesome and lead to harm (AN 3.65).

name: How a teacher is to be tested

definitions.definition: A monk investigates the Tathāgata over time for defiled, mixed or bright states and his conduct under fame (MN 47); a student examines a teacher for states based on greed, hatred and delusion before placing faith (MN 95); faith then grows through approach, listening and practice (MN 70).
Saying 'this is my faith' without concluding 'only this is true' (MN 95).

The teacher is unmoved whether disciples listen or not (MN 137); he does not treat disciples as a potter the raw clay but repeatedly admonishes (MN 122); the Tathāgata only points the way (MN 107; Dhp 276); good friendship is the whole of the holy life (SN 45.2).

name: The Dhamma and discipline as teacher

definitions.definition: After the Buddha's death the Dhamma and discipline he taught are to be the teacher (DN 16); monks are to be islands to themselves (DN 16; SN 47.13).

name: Oneself as island, the Dhamma as island

definitions.definition: 'Live as islands to yourselves, with no other refuge; with the Dhamma as island' — by the four establishments of mindfulness (DN 16; SN 47.13; DN 26); 'oneself is one's own protector' (Dhp 160).
A teaching claimed from the Buddha, a Saṅgha, learned elders or one elder is checked against the discourses and the discipline (DN 16).
What leads to dispassion, release, dismantling, few wishes, contentment, seclusion, energy and unburdensomeness is the Dhamma and the Teacher's instruction (AN 8.53).
The Buddha to Vakkali: seeing the Dhamma is seeing the Buddha (SN 22.87); the Buddha is called one whose body is the Dhamma (dhammakāya) in DN 27.
Reciting the teaching together in numbered lists so that the holy life may last (DN 33), the model of the councils.

At Rājagaha after the parinibbāna, five hundred arahants under Mahākassapa recited the discipline (Upāli) and the Dhamma (Ānanda), declined to abolish the minor rules, and charged Ānanda with faults including advocating women's ordination (Cv 11).

relations.note: the councils as remembered by the several schools (U38)

definitions.definition: A century later at Vesālī seven hundred elders rejected the ten points of the Vajjian monks, including accepting gold and silver (Cv 12).

relations.note: the councils as remembered by the several schools (U38)

definitions.definition: 'Come, monk' ordination by the Buddha, then by the three refuges (Vin Mv 1.12), then by formal act of the Saṅgha; the nuns' ordination by both Saṅghas (Cv 10).

name: The ten reasons for laying down training rules

definitions.definition: The excellence and comfort of the Saṅgha, restraint of the shameless, ease of the well-behaved, restraint and prevention of effluents, faith of the faithless and increase of the faithful, endurance of the true Dhamma and support of the discipline (Vin Pār 1).
Four for monks — sexual intercourse, theft, killing a human or inciting death, falsely claiming superhuman states — entailing loss of monkhood (Vin Pār 1–4); eight for nuns.

The order of nuns founded when Mahāpajāpatī accepted the eight principles of respect (Cv 10.1; AN 8.51); the Buddha affirms women can realise the four fruits (Cv 10.1.3); its nuns' verses (Thig) and the foremost nuns (AN 1).

The eight rules accepted by Mahāpajāpatī as her ordination: a nun ordained a century bows to a monk ordained that day; no rains without monks; fortnightly asking; invitation and penance before both Saṅghas; ordination by both after two years' training; no abuse of monks; no admonishing of monks (Cv 10.1.4; AN 8.51).

name: Women and awakening

definitions.definition: Women who go forth can realise stream-entry to arahantship (Cv 10.1.3); the nuns Somā and Vajirā answer Māra that womanhood is irrelevant to the concentrated mind (SN 5.2; Thig 3.8); the Therīgāthā records arahant nuns; the canon also states that a woman cannot be a fully awakened Buddha (MN 115; AN 1.279) and the Buddhavaṃsa names maleness among the conditions of the Buddha-aspiration (Bv 2.59).

notes: Recorded faithfully with both kinds of statement; see dsp:women-caste-liberation (U50) and dsp:bhikkhuni-order.

name: The duration and decline of the true Dhamma

definitions.definition: The true Dhamma would have lasted a thousand years; with women's going forth it will last five hundred (Cv 10.1.6; AN 8.51); the monks' conditions of non-decline (DN 16).

relations.note: the commentarial doctrine of the decline of the Sāsana (U37)

definitions.definition: Seven conditions for the Vajjī republic and several sets for the monks — meeting in concord, keeping the rules, honouring elders, forest dwelling, mindfulness (DN 16).
'Whoever would attend on me should attend on the sick' (Vin Mv 8.26); the qualities of a good nurse.

name: Wandering for the welfare of the many

definitions.definition: 'Wander forth for the welfare and happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world' (Vin Mv 1.11).
All is burning — the senses, their objects, consciousness, contact and feeling — with the fires of lust, hatred and delusion and with birth, ageing and death (SN 35.28; Vin Mv 1.21).

name: 'In the seen only the seen' (the Bāhiya teaching)

definitions.definition: In the seen there will be only the seen, in the heard only the heard, in the sensed only the sensed, in the cognised only the cognised; then 'you' will not be 'by that' or 'in that', neither here nor beyond nor between: the end of suffering (Ud 1.10; SN 35.95).
The ordinary person struck by painful bodily feeling adds mental grief like a second dart; the noble disciple feels only the bodily one (SN 36.6).
Not reviving the past nor longing for the future, seeing with insight each present state; making the effort today, for death may come tomorrow (MN 131).
Seeking the unborn, unageing, deathless security from bondage rather than what is itself subject to birth and death (MN 26).
Where the Tathāgata was born, awakened, first taught and attained final nibbāna (DN 16).

Sāriputta's teaching to the dying Anāthapiṇḍika not to cling to anything seen, heard, sensed or cognised, nor to this world or the next (MN 143); the ten perceptions to the sick Girimānanda (AN 10.60); the Buddha's last words (DN 16).
Giving food and drink in the name of dead relatives, who wait outside the walls and live on what is given here (Khp 7 / Pv 1.5).
Beings reborn in the realm of ghosts through miserliness and wrongdoing, relieved by offerings given in their name (Pv; Khp 7); the ghost realm is one of the five destinations (MN 12).

Kamma is intention; its source is contact, its result threefold in time, its cessation the cessation of contact, the way the eightfold path (AN 6.63); beings are owners of their deeds (MN 135); dark, bright, mixed and neither (AN 4.232); the same deed ripens differently in the developed and undeveloped (AN 3.100); not everything felt is due to past deeds (MN 101; AN 3.61).

relations.note: the shared Indian doctrine of action and result, defined here by intention
the Sarvāstivāda/Sautrāntika treatment (U38)

definitions.definition: Dark with dark result, bright with bright result, dark-and-bright, and neither dark nor bright, which leads to the destruction of kamma (AN 4.232–233).

Rebirth may follow an earlier deed, a later one, or the view at death, so those who see only part generalise wrongly (MN 136); results are graded by the doer's development (AN 3.100); kamma's results are unthinkable in detail (AN 4.77).

Beings pass away and reappear according to their deeds, seen with the divine eye (DN 2); conception requires the gandhabba (MN 38); the other world cannot be seen with the fleshly eye (DN 23); no self transmigrates — consciousness is dependently arisen (MN 38).

relations.note: rebirth without a transmigrating self, against Sāti's view (MN 38)

definitions.definition: The five destinations — hell, animals, ghosts, humans, gods (MN 12) — with the heavens of the sense sphere, the Brahmā worlds and the formless spheres; systematised in the commentaries as thirty-one planes (U37).

relations.note: the commentarial systematisation owned by U37

definitions.definition: Hell, the animal realm, the ghost realm, humans and gods, with the paths leading to each and to nibbāna (MN 12).
The realm of intense suffering in which beings experience the results of evil deeds, examined by King Yama (MN 130; MN 129).
A baby, an old person, a sick person, a criminal punished and a corpse, about which Yama questions the wrongdoer (MN 130; AN 3.36).
The realms of Brahmā reached by the brahmavihāras (DN 13) and the jhānas; Brahmās mistake their realm for permanent (MN 49; DN 1).
The guardian deities of the four directions, who offer the Āṭānāṭiya protection (DN 32) and first heard the proclamation of the wheel (SN 56.11).
The round of birth and death without discoverable beginning (SN 15.3); the tears shed exceed the four oceans.
The world contracts and expands over aeons; at contraction beings are mostly reborn in the Ābhassara realm (DN 27; DN 1).
The re-evolution of the world, the loss of the beings' radiance through craving for the savoury earth, the arising of sexes, property, the elected king and the four classes from occupations (DN 27).

relations.note: the Vedic origin of the classes from the cosmic Person's body (RV 10.90), rejected in DN 27

name: Decline and renewal of human life

definitions.definition: Human lifespan falls to ten years through neglect of Dhamma and rises to eighty thousand as virtue returns (DN 26).
A blind turtle surfacing once a century would put its neck through a yoke drifting on the ocean sooner than a fool gone to the lower realms would regain human birth (MN 129; SN 56.48).

The shock at seeing the world struggling like fish in a drying pool, which drove the Buddha to renounce (Snp 4.15); the four sights (DN 14); the four places of pilgrimage are sites of saṃvega (DN 16).

name: The blind men and the elephant

definitions.definition: Sectarians holding one-sided views quarrel like blind men each touching part of an elephant (Ud 6.4).
